scientific_question: Does the declared boundary-drive spectrum make aspect-ratio and screening changes distinguishable in response space?

metric.definition: G_ij = <partial B / partial theta_i, partial B / partial theta_j>_HS under the target observation measure and declared boundary-drive variances.
metric.modal_response: f(d,xi) sin(m pi y), with d=a sqrt((m pi)^2+lambda^2)
metric.interpretation: rho near one means the two task directions produce nearly collinear first-order response changes and are hard to distinguish.

finite_source_displacement_corroboration.definition: Cosine between the exact finite response displacements B_P-B_T and B_G-B_T for the frozen source parameters.
finite_source_displacement_corroboration.scope: Only the designed spectrum distance-matches P and G. The alternative spectra are used here solely to test whether the angular-confounding conclusion survives finite source displacements.

numerical_verification.method: Gauss-Legendre quadrature in normalized streamwise coordinate; the transverse sine norm is integrated analytically.

scientific_conclusions: The amplified high-frequency band is what makes aspect-ratio and screening directions well separated in the proposed response metric.
Smooth boundary spectra make those directions nearly collinear, so a null or unstable source ordering there would not by itself refute the transfer hypothesis.
A natural-spectrum follow-up must predict loss of discriminating power from the response metric or choose a task family with better-separated response tangents.
This rectangle tests aspect-ratio alignment versus screening alignment; it does not by itself test broad morphology reuse versus broad physics reuse.
interpretation_limits: The metric is local at the declared target and describes first-order response changes.
It measures identifiability under one observation measure, not learned transfer.
A finite source displacement can depart from the tangent approximation; the exact response distances remain the finite-displacement control.
